canonical_statement: The review synthesizes renal physiology, loop-diuretic pharmacology, mechanisms of diuretic resistance, and available clinical data to guide diuretic use in heart failure.
Robust clinical-trial evidence guiding diuretic use in heart failure is sparse compared with the evidence base for many disease-modifying heart-failure therapies.

Heart failure promotes proximal sodium and water reabsorption through altered filtration fraction, venous pressure, neurohormonal activation, and related peritubular forces, reducing distal sodium delivery.

source_anchor.paragraph: Renal physiology and diuretic response — Glomerulus and proximal tubules

canonical_statement: In heart failure, both natriuresis and maximal free-water excretion are reduced through decreased tubular delivery and neurohormonal mechanisms.

source_anchor.paragraph: Renal physiology and diuretic response — Loop of Henle

canonical_statement: Heart failure is characterized by low distal tubular flow, high aldosterone activity, and often high vasopressin activity, all of which favor distal sodium and water retention.

source_anchor.paragraph: Renal physiology and diuretic response — Distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct

canonical_statement: Effective loop-diuretic action requires gastrointestinal absorption when given orally, renal delivery, secretion into the tubular lumen, and binding to the target transport protein.
The review lists approximate intravenous equipotent doses of furosemide 40 mg, bumetanide 1 mg, and torsemide 20 mg.
The review lists oral bioavailability as highly variable for furosemide (10–100%, average about 50%) and more complete for bumetanide and torsemide (80–100%).
Loop diuretics have a steep threshold-and-ceiling dose-response relationship, and the dose-response curve is shifted downward and to the right in acute decompensated heart failure.
A fixed intravenous-to-oral furosemide conversion is not well supported by direct clinical data; the review recommends determining oral dosing by clinical response.
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs can impair loop-diuretic secretion and blunt natriuretic responsiveness.

canonical_statement: Chronic kidney disease shifts the loop-diuretic dose-response curve to the right and reduces maximal absolute natriuresis, supporting use of higher doses when needed for adequate tubular drug delivery.

source_anchor.paragraph: Distribution of diuretic agents to their site of action

canonical_statement: The review finds little evidence that albumin infusion enhances natriuretic efficacy when serum albumin is above 2 g/dL.

source_anchor.paragraph: Volumes of distribution, metabolism, and half-lives

canonical_statement: Short loop-diuretic half-lives permit post-diuretic sodium retention after the drug effect wanes, which is a rationale for at least twice-daily dosing of short-acting agents.

source_anchor.paragraph: Volumes of distribution, metabolism, and half-lives

canonical_statement: Chronic loop-diuretic exposure increases distal nephron sodium-reabsorptive capacity and causes nephron remodeling, producing the braking phenomenon and contributing to diuretic resistance.
For chronic loop-diuretic therapy, the review recommends using the lowest dose that maintains effective volume control, with dose reduction when guideline-directed therapy permits.

For hospitalized patients already taking a loop diuretic, the review presents an initial intravenous dose around 2.5 times the outpatient oral daily dose; for loop-naive patients it presents furosemide 40–80 mg IV twice daily or equivalent as a reasonable empiric start.
A serum creatinine rise during decongestion, including increases up to about 0.5 mg/dL, does not by itself always require stopping or reducing loop-diuretic therapy when congestion persists.

The review reports that the DOSE trial randomized 308 patients in a 2×2 factorial design and that higher-dose furosemide improved several prespecified secondary decongestion measures while the coprimary symptom endpoint did not reach statistical significance.
The review reports no meaningful clinical-endpoint advantage of continuous furosemide infusion over twice-daily intravenous bolus dosing in the DOSE trial.
Diuretic resistance is qualitatively defined as an inadequate rate or quantity of natriuresis despite an adequate diuretic regimen.
Low diuretic efficiency is associated with worse outcomes, particularly when poor response occurs despite high loop-diuretic doses.
Weight loss and net urine output correlate poorly even in rigorous diuretic trials, limiting their reliability as sole measures of decongestion.

The review reports that 28% of patients in ROSE-AHF had positive sodium balance and that positive sodium balance was associated with increased 6-month mortality, even among patients with negative fluid balance.
Post-diuretic spot urine sodium concentrations below approximately 50–70 mmol/L are associated with worse kidney and heart-failure outcomes in observational studies summarized by the review.

Most mechanistic evidence on diuretic resistance derives from animal models or human studies in healthy, hypertensive, or chronic-kidney-disease populations rather than contemporary heart-failure cohorts.
In most heart-failure patients, mild-to-moderate reductions in cardiac output are not the dominant mechanism of diuretic resistance; intrarenal mechanisms are generally more important.
Using inotropes solely to improve diuresis is generally ineffective when there is no defined hemodynamic target such as hypotension or low-output heart failure.

Estimated glomerular filtration rate does not correlate well with net diuretic responsiveness in heart failure, and lower-eGFR patients may compensate with greater sodium excretion per functioning nephron.
Post-loop-of-Henle tubular mechanisms appear to make a major contribution to diuretic resistance in heart failure once adequate loop-diuretic doses are delivered.

Combination nephron blockade with a thiazide-type agent can produce robust diuresis but carries substantial risk of electrolyte abnormalities, and the optimal loop-diuretic threshold for adding combination therapy is uncertain.

The review proposes that a spot urine sodium below about 50 mmol/L or urine output below about 150 mL/h at 2 hours indicates inadequate loop-diuretic response and generally warrants dose escalation with reassessment.

The proposed titration algorithm repeats an effective loop-diuretic dose every 6–12 hours and escalates inadequate doses, often up to roughly 200–300 mg furosemide-equivalent boluses, before adding combination blockade.
The review reports that intravenous chlorothiazide was not superior to oral metolazone when added to loop-diuretic therapy in a prospective trial of diuretic resistance.
The review reports that high-dose spironolactone did not improve net urine output or weight change in ATHENA-HF, while noting that the studied population did not exhibit clear diuretic resistance.
The optimal chronic loop-diuretic agent was uncertain in 2020; the review noted pharmacokinetic advantages of torsemide but only limited outcome evidence and an ongoing pragmatic outcomes trial.

source_anchor.paragraph: Loop diuretic use in chronic HF

canonical_statement: The review reports that loop-diuretic withdrawal may be feasible in selected stable, low-risk heart-failure outpatients receiving optimized therapy and close follow-up.
Intermittent outpatient intravenous loop-diuretic treatment was considered potentially useful in selected high-risk patients, but systematic evidence for this strategy was limited.
Subcutaneous furosemide had pharmacokinetic and diuretic-response data in 2020, but the review noted a lack of clinical-outcome evidence.
Future research priorities include better definitions and treatments for diuretic resistance, prospective evaluation of urine-sodium-guided titration, and study of novel combination strategies.
Safe and effective diuretic therapy in heart failure requires integrating renal physiology with the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of diuretic agents.
Felker, Cox, and Testani reported multiple research, consulting, or personal financial relationships; the other authors reported no relationships relevant to the paper.
